name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q01 - Most important factor for halogen resemblance

questiontext.text: Hydrogen resembles halogens in many respects for which several factors are responsible. Of the following factors which one is most important in this respect?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Elements in the periodic table exhibit similar chemical properties primarily when they have similar valence-shell electronic configurations or require the same number of electrons to attain the nearest noble gas configuration.

Step 2: Evaluation
Hydrogen has the electronic configuration \(1s^1\). It is one electron short of the stable noble gas configuration of helium (\(1s^2\)). Similarly, halogens have the outer electronic configuration \(ns^2np^5\) and are one electron short of the nearest noble gas configuration (\(ns^2np^6\)).

Step 3: Application and Conclusion
Because of this electronic deficit, hydrogen shows a tendency to gain a single electron in its valence shell to form the hydride ion (\(\mathrm{H}^-\)) and attain a stable noble gas configuration, just as halogens gain one electron to form halide ions (\(\mathrm{X}^-\)). Therefore, the most important factor responsible for hydrogen's resemblance to halogens is its tendency to gain a single electron in its valence shell to attain stable electronic configuration.

answer.text: Its tendency to lose an electron to form a cation.
Its tendency to gain a single electron in its valence shell to attain stable electronic configuration.
Its low negative electron gain enthalpy value.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q02 - Association of hydrogen ion with molecules

questiontext.text: Why does \(\mathrm{H}^+\) ion always get associated with other atoms or molecules?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A neutral hydrogen atom consists of one proton and one electron. When it loses its single electron, only a bare proton (\(\mathrm{H}^+\)) remains.

Step 2: Evaluation
The radius of a bare proton (\(\mathrm{H}^+\)) is approximately \(1.5 \times 10^{-3}\text{ pm}\), which is extremely small compared to normal atomic and ionic radii (\(50\text{ to }200\text{ pm}\)). Consequently, the \(\mathrm{H}^+\) ion has an extraordinarily high charge-to-size ratio (charge density) and intense polarising power.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Due to its very small size, \(\mathrm{H}^+\) cannot exist free and immediately associates with other atoms or molecules (for example, forming \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+\) in water). Thus, loss of an electron from a hydrogen atom results in a nucleus of very small size as compared to other atoms or ions, and due to this small size it cannot exist free.

answer.text: Ionisation enthalpy of hydrogen resembles that of alkali metals.
It resembles both alkali metals and halogens.
Loss of an electron from hydrogen atom results in a nucleus of very small size as compared to other atoms or ions. Due to small size it cannot exist free.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q03 - Increasing ionic character of alkali hydrides

questiontext.text: Metal hydrides are ionic, covalent or molecular in nature. Among \(\mathrm{LiH}\), \(\mathrm{NaH}\), \(\mathrm{KH}\), \(\mathrm{RbH}\), \(\mathrm{CsH}\), the correct order of increasing ionic character is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Fajan's rules and electronegativity trends, the ionic character of a binary compound \(\mathrm{MH}\) increases as the electropositive character of the metal \(\mathrm{M}\) increases (or as the polarising power of the cation \(\mathrm{M}^+\) decreases).

Step 2: Evaluation
In Group 1 (alkali metals), atomic size increases down the group from \(\mathrm{Li}\) to \(\mathrm{Cs}\), while ionisation enthalpy and electronegativity decrease. Consequently, the electropositive character increases in the order \(\mathrm{Li} < \mathrm{Na} < \mathrm{K} < \mathrm{Rb} < \mathrm{Cs}\), and the polarising power of \(\mathrm{M}^+\) decreases from \(\mathrm{Li}^+\) to \(\mathrm{Cs}^+\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the covalent character decreases and the ionic character increases down the group, giving the increasing order of ionic character as \(\mathrm{LiH} < \mathrm{NaH} < \mathrm{KH} < \mathrm{RbH} < \mathrm{CsH}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q04 - Identification of electron precise hydride

questiontext.text: Which of the following hydrides is electron-precise hydride?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Covalent (molecular) hydrides are classified into three categories based on the number of electrons around the central atom: electron-deficient (fewer electrons than needed for a conventional Lewis octet), electron-precise (exact number of electrons required to form normal covalent bonds), and electron-rich (excess electrons present as lone pairs).

Step 2: Evaluation
\(\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{H}_6\) (a Group 13 hydride) is electron-deficient because boron has fewer than 8 valence electrons in \(\mathrm{BH}_3\). \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) (Group 15) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) (Group 16) are electron-rich hydrides because the central atoms possess one and two lone pairs of electrons, respectively. In \(\mathrm{CH}_4\) (Group 14), carbon has 4 valence electrons and forms 4 covalent \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds, giving an exact octet with no lone pairs.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, \(\mathrm{CH}_4\) is an electron-precise hydride.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q05 - Radioactive isotope of hydrogen

questiontext.text: Radioactive elements emit \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) rays and are characterised by their half-lives. The radioactive isotope of hydrogen is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hydrogen has three naturally occurring isotopes differing in the number of neutrons in their nuclei: protium (\({}_1^1\mathrm{H}\), 0 neutrons), deuterium (\({}_1^2\mathrm{H}\) or \(\mathrm{D}\), 1 neutron), and tritium (\({}_1^3\mathrm{H}\) or \(\mathrm{T}\), 2 neutrons).

Step 2: Evaluation
Protium and deuterium are stable, non-radioactive isotopes. Tritium has an unstable nucleus with a neutron-to-proton ratio of \(2:1\) and undergoes \(\beta^-\) decay with a half-life of \(12.33\text{ years}\). Hydronium (\(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+\)) is a polyatomic cation, not an isotope of hydrogen.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the radioactive isotope of hydrogen is Tritium.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q06 - Redox behaviour of hydrogen peroxide

questiontext.text:
Consider the reactions

(A) \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 + 2\mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow \mathrm{I}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)

(B) \(\mathrm{HOCl} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+ + \mathrm{Cl}^- + \mathrm{O}_2\)

Which of the following statements is correct about \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) with reference to these reactions? Hydrogen peroxide is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An oxidising agent is a substance that oxidises another species (increasing its oxidation state) while itself getting reduced (decreasing its oxidation state). A reducing agent reduces another species while itself getting oxidised.

Step 2: Evaluation of the First Reaction
In \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 + 2\mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow \mathrm{I}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\), the oxidation state of iodine increases from \(-1\) in \(\mathrm{HI}\) to \(0\) in \(\mathrm{I}_2\), while the oxidation state of oxygen in \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) decreases from \(-1\) to \(-2\) in \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\). Thus, \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) oxidises \(\mathrm{HI}\) to \(\mathrm{I}_2\) and acts as an oxidising agent.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Second Reaction
In \(\mathrm{HOCl} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+ + \mathrm{Cl}^- + \mathrm{O}_2\), the oxidation state of chlorine decreases from \(+1\) in \(\mathrm{HOCl}\) to \(-1\) in \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\), while the oxidation state of oxygen in \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) increases from \(-1\) to \(0\) in \(\mathrm{O}_2\). Thus, \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) reduces \(\mathrm{HOCl}\) to \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\) and acts as a reducing agent.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, hydrogen peroxide is an oxidising agent in (A) and a reducing agent in (B).

answer.text: an oxidising agent in (A) and reducing agent in (B)
a reducing agent in (A) and oxidising agent in (B)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q07 - Oxide yielding hydrogen peroxide with acid

questiontext.text: The oxide that gives \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) on treatment with dilute \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Peroxides contain the \(\mathrm{O}_2^{2-}\) ion (oxygen in the \(-1\) oxidation state) and yield hydrogen peroxide (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\)) when treated with dilute mineral acids. Dioxides such as \(\mathrm{PbO}_2\), \(\mathrm{MnO}_2\), and \(\mathrm{TiO}_2\) contain \(\mathrm{O}^{2-}\) ions (oxygen in the \(-2\) oxidation state) and do not contain the peroxo linkage.

Step 2: Evaluation
Hydrated barium peroxide, \(\mathrm{BaO}_2\cdot 8\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\), is a true peroxide containing the \(\mathrm{O}_2^{2-}\) ion. On acidification with dilute \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\), it reacts to form insoluble barium sulphate and hydrogen peroxide:

\[\mathrm{BaO}_2\cdot 8\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4(\mathrm{aq}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{BaSO}_4(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{aq}) + 8\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l})\]

In contrast, \(\mathrm{PbO}_2\), \(\mathrm{MnO}_2\), and \(\mathrm{TiO}_2\) are dioxides and do not produce \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) with dilute \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, the oxide that gives \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) on treatment with dilute \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) is \(\mathrm{BaO}_2\cdot 8\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + \mathrm{O}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q08 - Equation depicting oxidising nature of peroxide

questiontext.text: Which of the following equations depict the oxidising nature of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) acts as an oxidising agent when the oxidation state of oxygen in \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) decreases from \(-1\) to \(-2\) (forming \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) or \(\mathrm{OH}^-\)), while the other reactant is oxidised to a higher oxidation state. When \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) acts as a reducing agent, it is oxidised to \(\mathrm{O}_2\) (oxidation state \(0\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
In \(2\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + 6\mathrm{H}^+ + 5\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + 8\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + 5\mathrm{O}_2\), \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^-\) (\(+7\)) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\) (\(+2\)), so \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) acts as a reducing agent. In \(2\mathrm{Fe}^{3+} + 2\mathrm{H}^+ + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + \mathrm{O}_2\), \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\), so \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) acts as a reducing agent. In \(\mathrm{KIO}_4 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 \longrightarrow \mathrm{KIO}_3 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + \mathrm{O}_2\), iodine is reduced from \(+7\) to \(+5\), so \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) acts as a reducing agent. However, in \(2\mathrm{I}^- + 2\mathrm{H}^+ + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 \longrightarrow \mathrm{I}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\), iodide (\(\mathrm{I}^-\), oxidation state \(-1\)) is oxidised to iodine (\(\mathrm{I}_2\), oxidation state \(0\)) while \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the equation \(2\mathrm{I}^- + 2\mathrm{H}^+ + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 \longrightarrow \mathrm{I}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) depicts the oxidising nature of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q09 - Equation depicting reducing nature of peroxide

questiontext.text: Which of the following equation depicts reducing nature of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) acts as a reducing agent when it reduces another species (decreasing that species' oxidation state) and is itself oxidised to \(\mathrm{O}_2\) (oxidation state of oxygen increases from \(-1\) to \(0\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
In \(2[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]^{4-} + 2\mathrm{H}^+ + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 \longrightarrow 2[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]^{3-} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\), iron is oxidised from \(+2\) to \(+3\), so \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) is an oxidising agent. In \(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{4+} + 2\mathrm{OH}^-\), manganese is oxidised from \(+2\) to \(+4\), so \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) is an oxidising agent. In \(\mathrm{PbS} + 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbSO}_4 + 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\), sulphur is oxidised from \(-2\) to \(+6\), so \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) is an oxidising agent. In \(\mathrm{I}_2 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 + 2\mathrm{OH}^- \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{I}^- + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + \mathrm{O}_2\), iodine is reduced from \(0\) in \(\mathrm{I}_2\) to \(-1\) in \(\mathrm{I}^-\) while \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{O}_2\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the equation \(\mathrm{I}_2 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 + 2\mathrm{OH}^- \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{I}^- + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + \mathrm{O}_2\) depicts the reducing nature of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q10 - Dual redox nature of hydrogen peroxide

questiontext.text: Hydrogen peroxide is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In hydrogen peroxide (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\)), oxygen has an oxidation state of \(-1\), which is intermediate between the minimum oxidation state of \(-2\) (as in \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)) and the maximum common oxidation state of \(0\) (as in \(\mathrm{O}_2\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
Because \(-1\) is an intermediate oxidation state, \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) can be reduced to \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) (acting as an oxidising agent) and can also be oxidised to \(\mathrm{O}_2\) (acting as a reducing agent) in both acidic and basic media.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, hydrogen peroxide is both an oxidising and a reducing agent.

answer.text: both an oxidising and a reducing agent

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q11 - Increasing dihydrogen from synthesis gas

questiontext.text: Which of the following reactions increases production of dihydrogen from synthesis gas?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Synthesis gas (syngas) is a mixture of carbon monoxide (\(\mathrm{CO}\)) and dihydrogen (\(\mathrm{H}_2\)). To increase the yield of \(\mathrm{H}_2\) from syngas, the \(\mathrm{CO}\) present in syngas is reacted with steam in the water-gas shift reaction.

Step 2: Evaluation
The reactions of \(\mathrm{CH}_4\), \(\mathrm{C}\), and \(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_6\) with steam at \(1270\text{ K}\) produce synthesis gas (water gas) rather than increasing \(\mathrm{H}_2\) from already formed synthesis gas. In contrast, the water-gas shift reaction converts \(\mathrm{CO}\) in synthesis gas with steam at \(673\text{ K}\) in the presence of an iron chromate catalyst into \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) and additional \(\mathrm{H}_2\):

\[\mathrm{CO}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{g}) \xrightarrow[\text{Catalyst}]{673\text{ K}} \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g})\]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, the water-gas shift reaction \(\mathrm{CO}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{g}) \xrightarrow[\text{Catalyst}]{673\text{ K}} \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g})\) increases the production of dihydrogen from synthesis gas.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q12 - Reaction of sodium peroxide with acid

questiontext.text: When sodium peroxide is treated with dilute sulphuric acid, we get

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sodium peroxide (\(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{O}_2\)) is an ionic peroxide containing the \(\mathrm{O}_2^{2-}\) ion. When metallic peroxides are treated with cold dilute mineral acids, they undergo a double-displacement reaction to form the corresponding metal salt and hydrogen peroxide.

Step 2: Evaluation
Treating sodium peroxide with dilute sulphuric acid yields sodium sulphate and hydrogen peroxide according to the balanced chemical equation:

\[\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4(\mathrm{aq}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{SO}_4(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{aq})\]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, we get sodium sulphate and hydrogen peroxide.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q13 - Preparation of hydrogen peroxide by electrolysis

questiontext.text: Hydrogen peroxide is obtained by the electrolysis of

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the electrolytic method for preparing hydrogen peroxide, an acidified sulphate solution (such as \(50\%\) sulphuric acid) is electrolysed at high current density to form peroxodisulphuric acid, which is then hydrolysed.

Step 2: Evaluation
During electrolysis of sulphuric acid, \(\mathrm{HSO}_4^-\) ions are oxidised at the anode to peroxodisulphuric acid (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_8\)), which upon distillation with water hydrolyses to give hydrogen peroxide:

\[2\mathrm{HSO}_4^-(\mathrm{aq}) \xrightarrow{\text{Electrolysis}} \mathrm{HO}_3\mathrm{SOOSO}_3\mathrm{H}(\mathrm{aq}) \xrightarrow{\text{Hydrolysis}} 2\mathrm{HSO}_4^-(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{H}^+(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{aq})\]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, hydrogen peroxide is obtained by the electrolysis of sulphuric acid.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q14 - Use of water gas in synthesis

questiontext.text: Which of the following reactions is an example of use of water gas in the synthesis of other compounds?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Water gas (or synthesis gas) is an equimolar mixture of \(\mathrm{CO}\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\). When it is used directly as a reactant to synthesise organic chemicals such as methanol, that reaction illustrates its synthetic utility.

Step 2: Evaluation
The reactions of \(\mathrm{CH}_4\) or alkanes (\(\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n+2}\)) with steam produce water gas/syngas, while the reaction of \(\mathrm{CO}\) with steam is the water-gas shift reaction used to increase \(\mathrm{H}_2\) yield. In contrast, the catalytic hydrogenation of carbon monoxide in water gas over a cobalt catalyst synthesises methanol:

\[\mathrm{CO}(\mathrm{g}) + 2\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g}) \xrightarrow[\text{Catalyst}]{\text{Cobalt}} \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{OH}(\mathrm{l})\]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the synthesis of methanol from \(\mathrm{CO}(\mathrm{g}) + 2\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g})\) in the presence of a cobalt catalyst is an example of the use of water gas in the synthesis of other compounds.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q15 - Ion causing hardness in water

questiontext.text: Which of the following ions will cause hardness in water sample?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hardness of water is caused by the presence of dissolved multivalent cations, primarily calcium (\(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\)) and magnesium (\(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\)) ions, in the form of their hydrogen carbonates, chlorides, and sulphates. These ions react with soap (sodium stearate) to form insoluble precipitates (scum).

Step 2: Evaluation
Alkali metal ions such as \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) and \(\mathrm{K}^+\), as well as anions such as \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\), form soluble salts with soap and do not cause hardness. In contrast, \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) precipitates soap as insoluble calcium stearate.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) ions cause hardness in a water sample.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q16 - Compound used for water softening

questiontext.text: Which of the following compounds is used for water softening?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Permanent hardness of water is removed by sequestering \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\) ions into soluble complexes or precipitating them out of solution.

Step 2: Evaluation
Sodium hexametaphosphate, \(\mathrm{Na}_6\mathrm{P}_6\mathrm{O}_{18}\) (commercially known as Calgon), is widely used for water softening. When added to hard water, it forms soluble complexes with \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\) ions, keeping them from precipitating with soap:

\[\mathrm{Na}_6\mathrm{P}_6\mathrm{O}_{18} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Na}^+ + \mathrm{Na}_4\mathrm{P}_6\mathrm{O}_{18}^{2-}\]

\[\mathrm{M}^{2+} + \mathrm{Na}_4\mathrm{P}_6\mathrm{O}_{18}^{2-} \longrightarrow [\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{MP}_6\mathrm{O}_{18}]^{2-} + 2\mathrm{Na}^+ \quad (\mathrm{M} = \mathrm{Mg}, \mathrm{Ca})\]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, \(\mathrm{Na}_6\mathrm{P}_6\mathrm{O}_{18}\) is used for water softening.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q17 - Periodic table groups forming no hydrides

questiontext.text: Elements of which of the following group(s) of periodic table do not form hydrides.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Many \(d\)-block and \(f\)-block elements react with hydrogen to form metallic (interstitial) hydrides. However, there is a region in the middle of the \(d\)-block known as the "hydride gap" where metals do not form hydrides.

Step 2: Evaluation
Metals belonging to Groups 7, 8, and 9 of the periodic table do not form hydrides due to their low affinity for hydrogen. In contrast, elements of Groups 13, 14, 15, 16, and 17 form covalent (molecular) hydrides.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, elements of Groups 7, 8, 9 do not form hydrides.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q18 - Only one element forming hydride

questiontext.text: Only one element of ______ forms hydride.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the \(d\)-block, metals of Groups 7, 8, and 9 do not form hydrides (the hydride gap). Adjacent to this gap lies Group 6.

Step 2: Evaluation
Among the elements of Group 6 (chromium, molybdenum, and tungsten), only chromium forms a hydride (\(\mathrm{CrH}\)), whereas molybdenum and tungsten do not form hydrides. Elements of Groups 7, 8, and 9 form no hydrides at all.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, only one element of group 6 forms hydride.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQII_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q19 - False statements about hydrogen

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements are not true for hydrogen?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hydrogen has electronic configuration \(1s^1\), exists as a diatomic molecule \(\mathrm{H}_2\), and has a very high first ionisation enthalpy (\(1312\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Statement
Hydrogen exists as a diatomic molecule (\(\mathrm{H}_2\)) and has one electron in its outermost \(1s\) shell, so both of these statements are true. However, if hydrogen loses its single electron, it forms a bare proton (\(\mathrm{H}^+\)) of extremely small radius (\(\sim 1.5 \times 10^{-3}\text{ pm}\)) that cannot exist freely and immediately associates with other atoms or molecules. Furthermore, due to its very high ionisation enthalpy, hydrogen does not readily lose an electron to form ionic compounds; instead, it predominantly forms covalent compounds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the statements that are not true for hydrogen are that it can lose an electron to form a cation which can freely exist, and that it forms a large number of ionic compounds by losing an electron.

answer.text: It has one electron in the outermost shell.
It can lose an electron to form a cation which can freely exist
It forms a large number of ionic compounds by losing an electron.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQII_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q20 - Names of carbon monoxide hydrogen mixture

questiontext.text: Dihydrogen can be prepared on commercial scale by different methods. In its preparation by the action of steam on hydrocarbons, a mixture of \(\mathrm{CO}\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\) gas is formed. It is known as

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Passing steam over hydrocarbons or coke at high temperature (\(1270\text{ K}\)) produces a gaseous mixture of carbon monoxide (\(\mathrm{CO}\)) and dihydrogen (\(\mathrm{H}_2\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
The mixture of \(\mathrm{CO}\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\) is traditionally called water gas. Because it is used for the synthesis of methanol and a number of hydrocarbons, it is also called synthesis gas or syngas. Producer gas, by contrast, is a mixture of \(\mathrm{CO}\) and \(\mathrm{N}_2\), and "industrial gas" is not the specific name for this mixture.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, the mixture of \(\mathrm{CO}\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\) is known as both Water gas and Syngas.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQII_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q21 - Properties and uses of heavy water

questiontext.text: Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct in the case of heavy water?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Heavy water (\(\mathrm{D}_2\mathrm{O}\)) has a higher molecular mass (\(20.027\text{ g mol}^{-1}\)) than ordinary water (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\), \(18.015\text{ g mol}^{-1}\)) and forms slightly stronger intermolecular deuterium bonds.

Step 2: Evaluation
Heavy water is extensively used as a moderator in nuclear reactors to slow down fast-moving neutrons. Due to stronger intermolecular association (higher enthalpy of vaporisation and higher viscosity), heavy water is more associated than ordinary water. Because of this stronger association and higher molecular mass, heavy water has a higher boiling point (\(374.4\text{ K}\)) than ordinary water (\(373.0\text{ K}\)). Moreover, ordinary water has a higher dielectric constant than heavy water, making ordinary water a more effective solvent.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct statements are that heavy water is used as a moderator in nuclear reactor and that heavy water is more associated than ordinary water.

answer.text: Heavy water is used as a moderator in nuclear reactor.
Heavy water is more effective as solvent than ordinary water.
Heavy water is more associated than ordinary water.
Heavy water has lower boiling point than ordinary water.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQII_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q22 - Correct statements about hydrogen

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements about hydrogen are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hydrogen exists as three isotopes (protium, deuterium, and tritium), forms a bare proton \(\mathrm{H}^+\) of tiny size upon losing an electron, and acts as a strong reducing agent in many chemical reactions.

Step 2: Evaluation
Protium (\({}_1^1\mathrm{H}\)) accounts for about \(99.985\%\) of naturally occurring hydrogen, making it the most common of the three isotopes. Because \(\mathrm{H}^+\) has an extremely small nuclear radius (\(\sim 1.5 \times 10^{-3}\text{ pm}\)) and very high charge density, it cannot exist freely in solution (it forms \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+\)) and never acts as a free cation in ionic salts. On the other hand, dihydrogen readily acts as a reducing agent (for example, reducing metal oxides to metals).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct statements are that hydrogen has three isotopes of which protium is the most common, and hydrogen never acts as cation in ionic salts.

answer.text: Hydrogen has three isotopes of which protium is the most common.
Hydrogen never acts as cation in ionic salts.
Dihydrogen does not act as a reducing agent.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQII_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q23 - Incorrect properties of water and ice

questiontext.text: Some of the properties of water are described below. Which of them is/are not correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Water is a polar molecule with a high dielectric constant and forms extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonds in both the liquid and solid (ice) states.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because of its polarity and hydrogen-bonding ability, water dissolves a wide variety of substances and is known as a universal solvent; hydrogen bonding is also present to a large extent in liquid water. In the frozen state (ice), each water molecule is tetrahedrally surrounded by four other water molecules through extensive hydrogen bonding, creating an open cage-like structure with vacant spaces. Consequently, the density of ice is lower than that of liquid water, so ice floats on water rather than being heavier than liquid water.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the incorrect statements are that there is no hydrogen bonding in the frozen state of water, and that frozen water is heavier than liquid water.

answer.text: Water is known to be a universal solvent.
Hydrogen bonding is present to a large extent in liquid water.
There is no hydrogen bonding in the frozen state of water.
Frozen water is heavier than liquid water.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQII_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q24 - Causes of permanent hardness of water

questiontext.text: Hardness of water may be temporary or permanent. Permanent hardness is due to the presence of

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Temporary hardness of water is caused by dissolved hydrogen carbonates of calcium and magnesium, which can be removed by boiling. Permanent hardness cannot be removed by boiling and is caused by other soluble salts of calcium and magnesium.

Step 2: Evaluation
Permanent hardness arises from the presence of soluble chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium (\(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\), \(\mathrm{MgCl}_2\), \(\mathrm{CaSO}_4\), \(\mathrm{MgSO}_4\)) in water. Hydrogen carbonates of \(\mathrm{Ca}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg}\) cause temporary hardness, while carbonates of alkali metals do not cause hardness.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, permanent hardness is due to the presence of chlorides of \(\mathrm{Ca}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg}\) in water and sulphates of \(\mathrm{Ca}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg}\) in water.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQII_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q25 - Classification and geometry of molecular hydrides

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Molecular hydrides of \(p\)-block elements are classified by their valence electron count: Group 13 forms electron-deficient hydrides, Group 14 forms electron-precise hydrides, and Groups 15–17 form electron-rich hydrides.

Step 2: Evaluation
All elements of Group 14 form electron-precise hydrides (such as \(\mathrm{CH}_4\) and \(\mathrm{SiH}_4\)), which have the exact number of electrons required for four normal covalent bonds and adopt tetrahedral geometries (\(sp^3\) hybridisation). Elements of Group 15 form electron-rich hydrides (not electron-deficient), and electron-rich hydrides donate lone pairs to act as Lewis bases (not Lewis acids).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct statements are that all elements of group 14 form electron precise hydrides, and electron precise hydrides have tetrahedral geometries.

answer.text: Elements of group 15 form electron deficient hydrides.
All elements of group 14 form electron precise hydrides.
Electron rich hydrides can act as Lewis acids.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQII_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q26 - Lewis acid base nature of hydrides

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor (such as a species with an incomplete octet), whereas a Lewis base is an electron-pair donor (such as a species with one or more lone pairs).

Step 2: Evaluation
Hydrides of Group 13 (e.g., \(\mathrm{BH}_3\), \(\mathrm{AlH}_3\)) are electron-deficient because the central atom has an incomplete octet, so they accept an electron pair and act as Lewis acids. Hydrides of Group 14 (e.g., \(\mathrm{CH}_4\), \(\mathrm{SiH}_4\)) are electron-precise with complete octets and no lone pairs or vacant valence orbitals of low energy, so they are neither electron-deficient nor Lewis acids. Hydrides of Group 15 (e.g., \(\mathrm{NH}_3\), \(\mathrm{PH}_3\)) are electron-rich with a lone pair on the central atom and act as Lewis bases.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct statements are that hydrides of group 13 act as Lewis acids, and hydrides of group 15 act as Lewis bases.

answer.text: Hydrides of group 13 act as Lewis acids.
Hydrides of group 14 are electron deficient hydrides.
Hydrides of group 14 act as Lewis acids.
Hydrides of group 15 act as Lewis bases.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQII_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q27 - Properties of metallic and ionic hydrides

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Metallic (interstitial) hydrides are formed by many \(d\)-block and \(f\)-block elements, whereas ionic (saline) hydrides are stoichiometric compounds formed by highly electropositive \(s\)-block elements.

Step 2: Evaluation
Metallic hydrides are almost always non-stoichiometric (for example, \(\mathrm{LaH}_{2.87}\), \(\mathrm{TiH}_{1.5-1.8}\)), meaning they are deficient of hydrogen, and they conduct heat and electricity (though not as efficiently as their parent metals). Ionic hydrides are crystalline, non-volatile, and non-conducting in the solid state because their ions are fixed in the crystal lattice; they conduct electricity only in the molten state.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct statements are that metallic hydrides are deficient of hydrogen, metallic hydrides conduct heat and electricity, and ionic hydrides do not conduct electricity in solid state.

answer.text: Ionic hydrides do not conduct electricity in solid state.
Ionic hydrides are very good conductors of electricity in solid state.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_MATCHING_Q63 - Correlations for hydrogen and its compounds

questiontext.text:
63. Correlate the items listed in Column I with those listed in Column II. Find out as many correlations as you can.

Column I Column II
(i) Synthesis gas (a) \(\mathrm{Na}_2[\mathrm{Na}_4(\mathrm{PO}_3)_6]\)
(ii) Dihydrogen (b) Oxidising agent
(iii) Heavy water (c) Softening of water
(iv) Calgon (d) Reducing agent
(v) Hydrogen peroxide (e) Stoichiometric compounds of s-block elements
(vi) Salt like hydrides (f) Prolonged electrolysis of water
(g) \(\mathrm{Zn} + \mathrm{NaOH}\)
(h) \(\mathrm{Zn} + \text{dil. }\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\)
(i) Synthesis of methanol
(j) Mixture of \(\mathrm{CO}\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each chemical species or class in the first set has characteristic compositions, preparation methods, chemical behaviours, or industrial uses that correlate with one or more entries in the second set.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Species
1. Synthesis gas is a mixture of carbon monoxide and dihydrogen (\(\mathrm{CO} + \mathrm{H}_2\)) and is used in the industrial synthesis of methanol.
2. Dihydrogen acts as a reducing agent, is used along with carbon monoxide in the synthesis of methanol, and is prepared in the laboratory by reacting zinc with sodium hydroxide (\(\mathrm{Zn} + \mathrm{NaOH}\)) or with dilute sulphuric acid (\(\mathrm{Zn} + \text{dil. }\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\)).
3. Heavy water (\(\mathrm{D}_2\mathrm{O}\)) is obtained by the prolonged electrolysis of water.
4. Calgon is sodium hexametaphosphate, \(\mathrm{Na}_2[\mathrm{Na}_4(\mathrm{PO}_3)_6]\), which is used for softening hard water.
5. Hydrogen peroxide (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\)) acts as both an oxidising agent and a reducing agent in acidic as well as alkaline media.
6. Salt-like hydrides (ionic or saline hydrides) are stoichiometric compounds formed by dihydrogen with s-block elements.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The complete set of correlations is: Synthesis gas \(\rightarrow\) Synthesis of methanol, Mixture of \(\mathrm{CO}\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\); Dihydrogen \(\rightarrow\) Reducing agent, \(\mathrm{Zn} + \mathrm{NaOH}\), \(\mathrm{Zn} + \text{dil. }\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\), Synthesis of methanol; Heavy water \(\rightarrow\) Prolonged electrolysis of water; Calgon \(\rightarrow\) \(\mathrm{Na}_2[\mathrm{Na}_4(\mathrm{PO}_3)_6]\), Softening of water; Hydrogen peroxide \(\rightarrow\) Oxidising agent, Reducing agent; Salt like hydrides \(\rightarrow\) Stoichiometric compounds of s-block elements.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_MATCHING_Q64 - Properties and applications of hydrogen species

questiontext.text: 64. Match Column I with Column II for the given properties/applications mentioned therein.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different forms and compounds of hydrogen—atomic hydrogen, molecular dihydrogen, water, and hydrogen peroxide—exhibit distinct chemical reactivities and industrial or laboratory applications.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Item
1. Atomic hydrogen (\(\mathrm{H}\)) recombines on a metal surface to release a large amount of heat (around \(4000\text{ K}\)) and is used in atomic hydrogen torches for cutting and welding.
2. Dihydrogen (\(\mathrm{H}_2\)) reacts with alkenes and carbon monoxide in the hydroformylation of olefins to yield aldehydes, which are further reduced to alcohols.
3. Water (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)) reacts with sodium hydride (\(\mathrm{NaH}\)) to liberate dihydrogen gas (\(\mathrm{NaH} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaOH} + \mathrm{H}_2\)), so water is reduced to dihydrogen by \(\mathrm{NaH}\).
4. Hydrogen peroxide (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\)) in a \(30\%\) aqueous solution is marketed under the name perhydrol.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\mathrm{H}\) is used in cutting and welding, \(\mathrm{H}_2\) is used in hydroformylation of olefins, \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) can be reduced to dihydrogen by \(\mathrm{NaH}\), and \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) is used in the name of perhydrol.

answer.text: Can be used in cutting and welding.
Can be used in hydroformylation of olefin.
Can be reduced to dihydrogen by \(\mathrm{NaH}\).
Used in the name of perhydrol.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_MATCHING_Q65 - Terms and relevant properties of hydrogen compounds

questiontext.text: 65. Match the terms in Column I with the relevant item in Column II.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each process or chemical substance involving hydrogen and its compounds corresponds to a specific product, chemical role, molecular property, or technological application.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Item
1. Electrolysis of water decomposes water into dihydrogen at the cathode and dioxygen at the anode, producing hydrogen and oxygen.
2. Lithium aluminium hydride (\(\mathrm{LiAlH}_4\)) is a strong source of hydride ions and is widely used as a reducing agent in organic synthesis.
3. Hydrogen chloride (\(\mathrm{HCl}\)) has a large electronegativity difference between hydrogen and chlorine, making it a polar molecule.
4. Heavy water (\(\mathrm{D}_2\mathrm{O}\)) is used as a moderator in nuclear (atomic) reactors to slow down fast-moving neutrons.
5. Atomic hydrogen recombines on a metal surface to form \(\mathrm{H}_2\) molecules, releasing high energy that generates a very high temperature.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, electrolysis of water produces hydrogen and oxygen, lithium aluminium hydride is used as a reducing agent, hydrogen chloride is a polar molecule, heavy water is used in atomic reactors, and atomic hydrogen recombines on a metal surface to generate high temperature.

answer.text: recombines on metal surface to generate high temperature

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_MATCHING_Q66 - Uses of hydrogen peroxide and water softening

questiontext.text:
66. Match the items in Column I with the relevant item in Column II.

Column I Column II
(i) Hydrogen peroxide is used as a (a) zeolite
(ii) Used in Calgon method (b) perhydrol
(iii) Permanent hardness of hard water is removed by (c) sodium hexametaphosphate
(d) propellant

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hydrogen peroxide has important commercial and aerospace uses, while permanent hardness of water (caused by dissolved chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium) is removed by ion-exchange or complexing agents.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Item
1. Hydrogen peroxide (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\)) is used as a rocket propellant (in concentrated form, around \(90\%\)) and is also marketed as a \(30\%\) aqueous solution called perhydrol.
2. Calgon method uses sodium hexametaphosphate (\(\mathrm{Na}_6\mathrm{P}_6\mathrm{O}_{18}\)), commercially known as Calgon, to form soluble complexes with \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\) ions.
3. Permanent hardness of hard water is removed by both sodium aluminium silicate (zeolite/permutit) in the ion-exchange method and sodium hexametaphosphate in Calgon's method.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, hydrogen peroxide corresponds to perhydrol and propellant; the Calgon method uses sodium hexametaphosphate; and permanent hardness of hard water is removed by zeolite and sodium hexametaphosphate.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_ASSERTIONANDREASON_Q67 - Removal of permanent hardness using washing soda

questiontext.text:
67. Assertion (A) : Permanent hardness of water is removed by treatment with washing soda.

Reason (R) : Washing soda reacts with soluble magnesium and calcium sulphate to form insoluble carbonates.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Permanent hardness of water is caused by dissolved chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium (\(\mathrm{CaCl}_2, \mathrm{MgCl}_2, \mathrm{CaSO}_4, \mathrm{MgSO}_4\)), which cannot be removed by simple boiling.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion and Reason
When washing soda (sodium carbonate, \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\)) is added to hard water, it reacts with soluble calcium and magnesium sulphates (and chlorides) to precipitate insoluble calcium carbonate (\(\mathrm{CaCO}_3\)) and magnesium carbonate (\(\mathrm{MgCO}_3\)): \[\mathrm{MSO}_4 + \mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{MCO}_3\downarrow + \mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \quad (\text{where } \mathrm{M} = \mathrm{Ca}, \mathrm{Mg})\] Removing the \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\) ions as insoluble carbonates softens the water.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, and the precipitation of insoluble carbonates by washing soda is the exact reason why washing soda removes permanent hardness of water.

answer.text: Statements A and R both are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is correct but R is not correct.
A and R both are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_ASSERTIONANDREASON_Q68 - Platinum and palladium as hydrogen storage media

questiontext.text:
68. Assertion (A) : Some metals like platinum and palladium, can be used as storage media for hydrogen.

Reason (R) : Platinum and palladium can absorb large volumes of hydrogen.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Certain transition metals such as palladium (\(\mathrm{Pd}\)) and platinum (\(\mathrm{Pt}\)) exhibit occlusion, the property of absorbing or adsorbing large volumes of dihydrogen gas into their metallic crystal lattices.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion and Reason
Because platinum and palladium can absorb large volumes of hydrogen gas reversibly (forming interstitial/metallic hydrides), they serve as effective solid-state storage media for hydrogen.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, and the ability of platinum and palladium to absorb large volumes of hydrogen directly explains why they can be used as storage media for hydrogen.

answer.text: Statements A and R both are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is correct but R is not correct.
A and R both are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A.
